name: Curtains Over Blinds: Getting the Rod, Clearance and Fabric Layers Right
heading: Curtains Over Blinds: Getting the Rod, Clearance and Fabric Layers Right
title: Curtains Over Blinds: Planning Drapery | John Crawford
description: Plan curtains over blinds with advice on rod projection, fabric stack, lining and Carole Fabrics custom drapes from John Crawford Company.
excerpt: Plan curtains over blinds with advice on rod projection, fabric stack, lining and Carole Fabrics custom drapes from John Crawford Company.
author: John Crawford Company

cover.alt: Pale blue drapery beside a white-framed window, a sofa and a dark blue cabinet.
cover.caption: Carole Fabrics® Custom Drapes · Hunter Douglas

intro: Adding curtains over blinds can change the appearance of a room without making the blind responsible for every part of the window's look. The blind can handle daily light adjustments while the drapery brings fabric, color and another layer of coverage.

Before choosing the fabric, decide what the curtains need to do. Panels that remain at the sides require a different arrangement from drapes that close across the glass each evening. That decision guides the rod or track, the fabric and the space needed around the existing blind.

sections.heading: Side panels or curtains that close?

rows: Frame the window and add fabric
Cover the opening as well as frame it
Travel along a rod or track
The planned fullness at each side
The gathered fabric when fully open
The blind still supplies most coverage across the glass
Drapery can add coverage when closed
Support the panels at their fixed positions
Support the fabric and allow the full travel
table.caption: Side panels or curtains that close?

sections.heading: Measure what projects in front of the wall
paragraphs: An existing blind may have a valance, headrail or bracket that extends beyond the frame. A curtain rod needs enough projection for the fabric to hang and move in front of it. The deepest part of the existing treatment is more useful than the glass alone when planning that clearance.

The controls need access, too. A curtain panel should not make the blind difficult to operate or catch on its hardware. If the window has a handle or opens into the room, we include that movement in the layout.

sections.heading: Allow for the fabric when the curtains are open
paragraphs: Fabric gathers at the sides when drapery opens. The amount of space it occupies depends on the material, fullness, heading style and hardware. That gathered fabric can cover part of the glass if there is limited wall space beside the window.

We look at the available space before setting the rod width. A nearby corner, cabinet or doorway may limit where the fabric can sit. A symmetrical arrangement may look appealing on paper but need adjusting around the actual room.

sections.heading: Choose fabric and lining for their separate roles
paragraphs: Color and texture affect the appearance of the drapery. Lining influences how it hangs, how much light passes through and the coverage it provides. Compare the combination rather than selecting the face fabric first and treating the lining as an afterthought.

Carole Fabrics, a Hunter Douglas partner company, offers custom drapes and side panels in pleated, non-pleated and Ripplefold styles, with hardware and decorative trim options. That gives you choices in how the fabric forms at the top and falls beside the blind.

A patterned drape can work with a quiet blind finish, while a textured solid can add interest without another large pattern. Samples are helpful beside your existing rug, upholstery and window treatment.

sections.heading: Use the layers to address the light you want to change
paragraphs: Describe the specific problem: an exposed room after dark, morning light at the sides of a bedroom blind, or a window that needs fabric around it. The answer may involve different drapery coverage or lining depending on that need.

Stationary panels alone will not close across the glass. If evening coverage is part of the goal, plan working drapery or another suitable treatment. For a darker bedroom, the arrangement around the sides and top deserves attention along with the fabrics.

sections.heading: Plan the complete window before ordering
paragraphs: Existing blinds do not all need replacing to add drapery. We first review their condition, the mounting space and the way the new layers will operate. The rod or track must support the chosen fabric and allow the movement you expect.

John Crawford Company helps with custom drapery fabric, lining and hardware selection as well as measuring and installation. Arrange a Woodland Hills showroom appointment or an in-home consultation to plan the layers around the blinds you already have.

name: Wood vs. Composite Shutters: Heritance or NewStyle?
heading: Wood vs. Composite Shutters: Heritance or NewStyle?
title: Wood vs. Composite Shutters | Heritance & NewStyle
description: Compare Hunter Douglas Heritance wood shutters and NewStyle composite shutters, including finishes, louver sizes, panel layout and window clearance.
excerpt: Compare Hunter Douglas Heritance wood shutters and NewStyle composite shutters, including finishes, louver sizes, panel layout and window clearance.
author: John Crawford Company

cover.alt: Dark wood shutters across a wide window wall beside a dining table and kitchen.
cover.caption: Hunter Douglas Heritance® Wood Shutters

intro: The material is one decision in a shutter project. The finish, louver size and panel layout determine much of what you will see and how comfortably the shutters will open around the room.

For Hunter Douglas, Heritance Wood Shutters and NewStyle Composite Shutters offer two ways to create a fitted interior shutter. Comparing wood vs. composite shutters is most useful when you look at these choices together rather than choosing a material before considering the window.

sections.heading: The material and finish differ

rows: Painted or stained wood; custom options available
Low-luster finish with a painted-wood appearance
Grain, stain or paint beside existing woodwork
Finish color and sheen beside trim and furnishings
Frame fit, panel layout and opening clearance
Frame fit, panel layout and opening clearance
table.caption: The material and finish differ

sections.heading: Consider Heritance when the wood finish matters
paragraphs: Heritance shutters are made from natural hardwood and offer painted and stained finishes, including custom paint and stain options. They deserve a close look if you want visible wood grain or are coordinating with cabinetry, furniture or an existing wood finish.

Compare the actual finish samples in the room. A stain can look different beside a wood floor than it does on its own. You may prefer a close relationship between the tones, or you may want the shutters to stand apart as a window feature.
Painted wood is another possibility. Choosing a painted appearance does not automatically settle the material question; it gives you a reason to compare both collections side by side.

sections.heading: Look at NewStyle for its composite construction
paragraphs: NewStyle shutters combine composite materials with a low-luster finish intended to resemble finely painted wood. Hunter Douglas positions the collection around durability as well as appearance.
Assess the finish where it meets the frame and surrounding trim. Two similar whites can differ in warmth or sheen. The room's daylight can make those differences easier to see than a photograph does.

Both Heritance and NewStyle have several louver sizes. That allows the material choice and the scale of the louvers to be considered separately rather than assuming a particular material requires a particular look.

sections.heading: Plan how the panels will open
paragraphs: A shutter panel occupies space as it swings into the room. Nearby furniture, a deep sill or a projecting window handle can affect the arrangement. The number of panels also changes the pattern across the glass and where the panel edges fall.

Think about how often you expect to open the entire panel. If you usually adjust only the louvers, the priorities may differ from a window you regularly open for air or cleaning. We check the movement you need while reviewing the layout.

sections.heading: Louver size affects more than the closed appearance
paragraphs: Broader louvers create a different pattern and view between them when open. They also need room to rotate without hitting handles or glass. Frame depth and the available mounting position help determine which arrangements work.

For a bedroom, discuss the darkness you expect. Shutters can reduce incoming light, but small gaps around panels and louvers may remain visible. We review coverage and whether another layer would suit your needs.

sections.heading: Include the room's exposure in the discussion
paragraphs: Tell us about moisture and strong sunlight before choosing. A bathroom or a particularly exposed window may call for another material comparison. Hunter Douglas Palm Beach Polysatin Vinyl Shutters are a separate vinyl option designed for those conditions; they are not the same material as NewStyle composite shutters.

From our Woodland Hills showroom, John Crawford Company helps compare shutter materials, finishes and panel arrangements, with measuring and installation handled by our team. An appointment gives us a chance to look at the window as well as the finish you like.

name: Do Woven Wood Shades Need a Liner? A Closer Look at Provenance
heading: Do Woven Wood Shades Need a Liner? A Closer Look at Provenance
title: Woven Wood Shades With a Liner | Provenance Guide
description: Explore Hunter Douglas Provenance woven wood shades with and without a liner. Compare privacy, daylight and independent liner options for your room.
excerpt: Explore Hunter Douglas Provenance woven wood shades with and without a liner. Compare privacy, daylight and independent liner options for your room.
author: John Crawford Company

cover.alt: Natural woven shades over tall windows beside a sofa and wood-framed lounge chair.
cover.caption: Hunter Douglas Provenance® Woven Wood Shades

intro: The weave that gives a natural shade its texture also affects how light passes through it. A material that looks substantial against a sample-book backing may reveal more openings when held in front of a bright window.

That is why choosing woven wood shades with a liner starts with the room's privacy needs and daylight. With Hunter Douglas Provenance Woven Wood Shades, an optional independent liner adds another way to control both while keeping the woven material as the front-facing treatment.

sections.heading: What the woven material contributes
paragraphs: Provenance shades are made from natural materials including woods, reeds, grasses and bamboo. The collection spans different weaves and textures, from airy materials to more opaque choices.

Look at the material against daylight as well as against a solid surface. You will get a better sense of the openings, the texture and the light entering through it. A sample's color is only part of the decision.

sections.heading: Compare the shade with and without a liner

rows: Adjusted through the weave and the separate liner
Assess the material in the room's lighting
Adds a separate layer to control coverage
The woven treatment is the primary layer
Liner operates independently from the front shade
Light passes directly through the weave
The backing can change how the weave and color appear
table.caption: Compare the shade with and without a liner

sections.heading: An independent liner gives the two layers different jobs
paragraphs: Hunter Douglas houses the Provenance independent liner within the shade's headrail while allowing it to operate separately from the woven shade. The liner is available in light-filtering and room-darkening opacities.

That means you can leave the woven material covering the window and change the layer behind it as your needs change. For example, the front shade can remain lowered while the liner is adjusted for additional coverage later in the day.

The liner also affects the appearance of the woven material. Compare the combination together: changing the backing can make the weave look more defined or alter how its color reads. The room-facing result should be part of the selection.

sections.heading: Nighttime privacy deserves a separate check
paragraphs: A daytime sample view does not answer every privacy question. Consider what is outside the window and how the room is used after dark. A dining room facing a neighbor's window can need more coverage than a room opening onto a private yard.

An open weave may not provide the evening coverage you expect by itself. We review the selected material and liner options with that use in mind. If privacy is a priority, say so before choosing a weave simply because you like its texture.

sections.heading: Room-darkening fabric is one part of a darker room
paragraphs: For a bedroom, a room-darkening liner can reduce light passing through the covered area. Light may still enter around the treatment's edges. Mounting position and coverage therefore need attention alongside the liner.

Existing drapery can be part of that discussion. It may offer another layer of coverage, but the shade, liner and curtains need room to move without interfering with one another. We check the arrangement before the order is finalized.

sections.heading: Match the liner to the way you use the room
paragraphs: A breakfast area may call for softer daylight during the morning, while a guest bedroom may need more flexible light reduction. The same woven texture does not require the same liner choice at every window.
We also discuss how you want to operate the layers and which controls are available for the selected configuration. At a tall window, access to those controls belongs in the planning from the start.

John Crawford Company helps you compare natural woven materials and liner choices during a free in-home consultation or a scheduled Woodland Hills showroom visit. Seeing the samples against your windows gives the texture, privacy and backing equal attention.

name: Silhouette vs. Pirouette: What Changes When the Vanes Open?
heading: Silhouette vs. Pirouette: What Changes When the Vanes Open?
title: Silhouette vs. Pirouette Shades | John Crawford
description: Compare Hunter Douglas Silhouette and Pirouette shades by vane design, view, daylight and room-darkening options before choosing your fabric.
excerpt: Compare Hunter Douglas Silhouette and Pirouette shades by vane design, view, daylight and room-darkening options before choosing your fabric.
author: John Crawford Company

cover.alt: Horizontal fabric vanes filtering light beside two lounge chairs and a pink sofa.
cover.caption: Hunter Douglas Silhouette® Sheer Shades

intro: A still photograph only shows one setting of a sheer shade. To understand the difference between Hunter Douglas Silhouette and Pirouette, it helps to watch the fabric vanes open and close, then look through them from where you normally sit.

Both collections combine fabric with a sheer layer to manage daylight and privacy. The way the vanes are arranged gives each a different appearance. That is the most useful place to start a Silhouette vs. Pirouette comparison.

sections.heading: The fabric is arranged differently

rows: S-shaped fabric vanes between two sheer layers
Fabric vanes attached to a single back sheer
Tilting vanes create spaces for filtered views
Fabric vanes change shape to reveal the back sheer
Selected Duolite or A Deux configurations
Vane spacing, fabric and the view through the sheers
The broader fabric vanes, their movement and the view
table.caption: The fabric is arranged differently

sections.heading: Silhouette creates a repeated horizontal pattern
paragraphs: Silhouette Sheer Shades hold their S-shaped fabric vanes between front and back sheer layers. Tilting the vanes changes the light passing through and your view outside.

The choice of vane size affects the scale of the treatment. A wider vane produces a different pattern across the window from a narrower one. Consider that pattern alongside window divisions, nearby shelving and other horizontal lines already in the room.

It is useful to view the sample from more than one position. What looks open when you stand directly in front of the window may read differently from a sofa or an adjoining room. Your normal viewing position should be part of the comparison.

sections.heading: Pirouette changes shape as the vanes open
paragraphs: Pirouette Sheer Shades use fabric vanes with a single sheer backing. Their broader vanes change shape as they open, giving the fabric a dimensional appearance. When comparing the two products, watch this movement rather than judging them only when fully closed.

Pirouette's 5-inch vanes create a different visual scale from the available Silhouette sizes. The fabric itself matters, too. A smooth material and a more visible texture can give the same construction a different character.

Neither appearance is automatically the better match for a large or small room. Consider how much you want the treatment to stand out and whether its pattern works with the furnishings you already have.

sections.heading: Compare the view and privacy as separate needs
paragraphs: Open vanes allow a filtered view through the sheer fabric. That view changes with the selected material, vane position and lighting. Ask to see the treatment both open and closed instead of assuming every sheer fabric will give the same result.

Evening privacy needs its own discussion. Tell us if the window faces a sidewalk, another house or an outdoor seating area. We can review what coverage you need when the room is lit and which configuration is appropriate.

sections.heading: A darker bedroom needs the right configuration
paragraphs: Both collections have selected configurations that combine the sheer treatment with a room-darkening roller behind it. Hunter Douglas offers Duolite or A Deux options for Silhouette and an A Deux option for Pirouette.

These are options to specify, not features to assume on every shade. We also consider light around the edges and the mounting arrangement when you want a darker room. Fabric, configuration and installation each contribute to the result.

sections.heading: Make the comparison from the room you use
paragraphs: Before choosing, note where you sit, when the sun is strongest and how often you expect to change the shade's position. Bring a photo showing the entire window wall so we can discuss the treatment alongside the rest of the room.

At John Crawford Company in Woodland Hills, we help compare Hunter Douglas shade fabrics and operating choices, then handle measuring and installation. Request an appointment to discuss Silhouette and Pirouette for your own windows.

name: Wood vs. Faux Wood Blinds: Parkland or EverWood for Your Room?
heading: Wood vs. Faux Wood Blinds: Parkland or EverWood for Your Room?
title: Wood vs. Faux Wood Blinds | Parkland & EverWood
description: Compare Hunter Douglas Parkland wood blinds and EverWood faux wood blinds for finish, moisture exposure, light control and window fit.
excerpt: Compare Hunter Douglas Parkland wood blinds and EverWood faux wood blinds for finish, moisture exposure, light control and window fit.
author: John Crawford Company

cover.alt: Dark horizontal wood blinds across a bank of windows behind a white sofa.
cover.caption: Hunter Douglas Parkland® Wood Blinds

intro: Two white blinds can look similar from across a room. The decision between wood and faux wood becomes more useful when you consider what happens around the window: direct sun, bathroom humidity, nearby finishes and the way you open it each day.

Hunter Douglas Parkland Wood Blinds and EverWood Faux Wood Blinds offer different materials in a familiar horizontal style. Both let you tilt the slats for daylight and privacy. The choice begins with the room and the finish you want to see.

sections.heading: Parkland and EverWood at a glance

rows: Painted finishes or stains that show wood grain
The room's sunlight and moisture conditions
Designed to resist humidity, fading and warping
Tilt the slats or raise the blind
Tilt the slats or raise the blind
table.caption: Parkland and EverWood at a glance

sections.heading: Start with the finish beside the window
paragraphs: Parkland is a natural starting point when visible wood grain is part of the look you want. Its stained finishes let the material contribute to the room alongside wood floors, furniture or trim. Painted wood is another option when you prefer a more uniform color.
EverWood provides a wood-style appearance in a different material. A painted look can coordinate across rooms even when exposure conditions lead you to use different products at different windows.

Compare finish samples with the surfaces that will stay in the room. A warm white blind can look different beside cooler white trim. For a stained blind, consider whether you want the wood tones to blend with your furniture or provide a deliberate contrast.

sections.heading: Treat moisture and sunlight as part of the product choice
paragraphs: A bathroom window and a living room window may need different materials. EverWood Faux Wood Blinds are designed to stand up to humidity and sunlight, with protection against fading, discoloration, warping and bowing. Those qualities make them worth comparing where moisture or strong sun affects the decision.

Tell us what the window is exposed to before settling on a finish. A room label alone does not explain the conditions: a kitchen window near steam can be different from one well away from the cooking area. We review the location and the product's suitability for it.

sections.heading: Slat size changes the appearance and the clearance
paragraphs: Both Parkland and EverWood offer 2-inch and 2½-inch slats. The broader slat changes the spacing you see when the blind is open and the horizontal pattern across the glass when it is closed.

The slats also need room to tilt. Window cranks, door handles and a shallow frame can affect how the blind is mounted. John Crawford Company measures the opening and checks those obstructions so the selection accounts for operation as well as appearance.

sections.heading: Decide whether you mostly tilt or fully raise the blind
paragraphs: Some people leave a blind lowered and adjust the slats as the light changes. Others raise it each morning to expose more glass. Think about your routine while comparing the controls and the fabric-free space you want at the window.

A raised horizontal blind leaves a stack of slats. Ask how that stack will sit at the top of your particular opening. For a bedroom, also discuss your expectations for darkness: closed slats reduce light, but gaps between slats and around the treatment can still admit it.

sections.heading: Choose for each room, then coordinate the result
paragraphs: Wood vs. faux wood blinds does not have to be a whole-house decision. Parkland may provide the grain you want in a sitting room, while EverWood suits the exposure in another space. Comparing the actual finishes helps keep those choices visually related.

John Crawford Company's blinds selection includes Hunter Douglas wood and faux wood options, with professional measuring and installation. Bring your room photos and finish ideas to an appointment at our Woodland Hills showroom, or arrange an in-home visit to compare samples where the blinds will be used.

name: Cellular Shades vs. Roller Shades: Duette or Designer Roller?
heading: Cellular Shades vs. Roller Shades: Duette or Designer Roller?
title: Cellular vs. Roller Shades | John Crawford Company
description: Compare Hunter Douglas Duette cellular shades and Designer Roller Shades for insulation, privacy, fabric choices and the fit at your windows.
excerpt: Compare Hunter Douglas Duette cellular shades and Designer Roller Shades for insulation, privacy, fabric choices and the fit at your windows.
author: John Crawford Company

cover.alt: Gray honeycomb shade across a wide bathroom window above a freestanding tub.
cover.caption: Hunter Douglas Duette® Honeycomb Shades

intro: Cellular shades are worth considering when you want added insulation at the window. Roller shades offer a flat fabric surface that can bring color, texture or pattern into the room. Both give you choices for managing daylight and privacy, but their construction changes how they look and operate.

For Hunter Douglas shoppers, that comparison often comes down to Duette Honeycomb Shades and Designer Roller Shades. Choosing between them gets easier when you look beyond the fabric sample and consider the shade fully lowered, partly open and raised.

sections.heading: What changes at the window?
paragraphs: A cellular shade has pleated fabric that forms pockets of air. A roller shade uses a continuous panel of fabric that wraps around a tube as it rises. Those differences remain visible as you use the shade throughout the day.

rows: A flat panel showing color, texture or pattern
A continuous fabric panel offers a simple appearance
table.caption: What changes at the window?

after: Neither style needs to be used throughout the entire house. A bedroom and a living room can call for different treatments, even when you want the rooms to feel connected.

sections.heading: Duette: consider comfort and flexible coverage
paragraphs: Duette Honeycomb Shades use a cellular structure that traps air within the fabric, adding insulation at the window. That construction deserves attention if the area beside your windows feels noticeably warmer or cooler than the rest of the room. The shade's fit and the window itself also affect comfort, so we consider the opening as part of the selection.
Duette shades have a pleated appearance when lowered. Look at that texture across the whole window, particularly if the room already has patterned upholstery, drapery or other fabrics.

Selected Duette configurations offer Top-Down/Bottom-Up operation. You can uncover glass at the top while keeping the lower portion covered, bringing daylight above eye level while maintaining coverage below. A window facing a walkway may benefit from that flexibility more than one overlooking a private garden.

sections.heading: Designer Roller: give the fabric a closer look
paragraphs: Designer Roller Shades offer fabrics ranging from sheer to opaque, with textures, prints and patterns. Because the lowered shade presents a flat area of fabric, the material has a strong influence on its appearance. A quiet neutral can sit alongside patterned furnishings. A more visible weave or print can make the window a feature of the room.
Compare samples with the shade lowered in mind. A small pattern that looks subtle in a sample book may become more noticeable across a broad window.
The finish at the top deserves attention, too. Discuss how the roll and selected hardware will look, especially if the shade will sit beneath existing drapery or within a shallow frame.

sections.heading: Separate daylight, privacy and bedroom darkness
paragraphs: When comparing cellular shades vs. roller shades, the fabric choice can matter as much as the style. For a living room, you may want daylight to pass through while reducing its intensity. For a bedroom, you may prefer substantially less light. At a window facing the street, your first concern may be privacy after dark.

Ask how the selected material behaves when the room is lit at night. Room-darkening fabric addresses light passing through the material; coverage around the opening also matters. A narrow band of light beside a shade can be noticeable in a bedroom even when the fabric itself blocks light well.

sections.heading: Look at the window with the shade raised
paragraphs: The shade's appearance when open is easy to overlook while choosing a color. Cellular fabric gathers as it rises, while roller fabric wraps around its tube. The amount of glass left exposed depends on the dimensions, construction and mounting position.

John Crawford Company checks frame depth, window handles and mounting space alongside width and height. If you prefer motorized operation, we also review the available controls for your chosen shade and window size. The product and the installation need to work together.

sections.heading: Compare the choices in your own room
paragraphs: Schedule an appointment at John Crawford Company's Woodland Hills showroom in Los Angeles, or request a free in-home consultation to compare suitable fabrics beside your windows. We help with shade selection, measuring and installation.

name: How to Choose Window Treatments for Large Windows
heading: How to Choose Window Treatments for Large Windows
title: Window Treatments for Large Windows | John Crawford
description: Compare shades, panels, drapery and controls for large windows. John Crawford Company explains light, privacy, fit and options for your home.
excerpt: Compare shade layouts, fabrics, side-to-side treatments and controls for wide windows, tall windows and walls of glass.
author: John Crawford Company

cover.alt: Pale screen shades across large living room windows overlooking the ocean.
cover.caption: Hunter Douglas Designer Screen Shades

intro: A wide living room window, a tall picture window and a wall of glass can each need a different approach. The right window treatment depends on the light coming in, the privacy you want and how you’d like to use the windows each day.

At John Crawford Company, we help you compare Hunter Douglas and Alta window treatments with those details in mind. Fabric and color are part of the choice. So are the arrangement, the controls and where the treatment will sit when it’s open.

sections.heading: Start with what you want to change about the room
paragraphs: Think about when your windows give you the most trouble. Afternoon sun might put glare across the television. A room that feels private during the day may feel exposed after dark. Or you may like the daylight and simply want to soften it.
Those situations call for different fabrics and levels of coverage.

If keeping the view is a priority, screen shades are worth considering. Their woven fabrics let you see through to varying degrees while filtering sunlight. Privacy changes with the lighting, though. When the room is lit at night, people outside may be able to see in. We’ll help you consider whether you need another layer for evening privacy.

For a bedroom, discuss how dark you want the room to feel. Light coming through the fabric and light entering around its edges are separate things. The mounting arrangement and coverage matter alongside the fabric you choose.

sections.heading: Compare one wide shade with several smaller shades
paragraphs: A large opening doesn’t always need one treatment across its entire width.

One wide shade gives you a continuous area of fabric. Several shades let you adjust different parts of the window separately. For example, you might lower the shade where the sun hits your seating area and leave the others open.

Window divisions can help guide the arrangement. On a row of three windows, individual shades may follow the frames naturally. Across one broad picture window, you’ll want to consider where the divisions between shades would fall.

Alta offers a two-on-one headrail arrangement for selected roller shades, allowing two shades to operate independently while sharing a continuous headrail. We can compare that approach with separate treatments and a single shade, depending on the opening and selected product.
Width, height, fabric and operating system all affect the available sizes. We check those details together when reviewing your windows.

sections.heading: Choose a treatment that suits the opening

subsections.heading: Roller and screen shades
paragraphs: Roller shades are a good starting point if you prefer a simple fabric treatment with little visual detail. Hunter Douglas Designer Roller Shades and Alta Roller Shades offer different fabrics and light-control choices.

Screen shades deserve a closer look when glare and the view are central to the decision. With a large area of glass, compare samples at the window so you can judge how clearly you can see outside and how much light comes through.

subsections.heading: Honeycomb shades
paragraphs: Honeycomb shades, also called cellular shades, are worth comparing when comfort is a concern. Their cellular construction traps air at the window, adding insulation.

Hunter Douglas Duette shades and Alta Honeycomb Shades offer different fabric and operating choices. We’ll help you compare the light control you want and the configurations available for your opening.

subsections.heading: Treatments that move from side to side
paragraphs: For a wide opening or sliding glass door, consider whether a treatment that travels sideways would be easier to use.

Hunter Douglas Luminette Sheer Panels combine sheer fabric with adjustable vertical vanes. Alta Panel Track shades use broad fabric panels that glide across the opening. They have different appearances and ways of controlling light, so seeing them operate can help you decide which you prefer.
If the opening includes a door, the treatment also needs to gather where it allows comfortable access.

sections.heading: Compare Hunter Douglas window treatments for large windows

rows.reason: A simple fabric treatment that keeps the window’s appearance uncluttered.
rows.light: Fabrics range from sheer to opaque, with different levels of light control and privacy.
rows.planning: Compare one wide shade with several smaller shades. Consider light entering around the fabric’s edges.

rows.reason: Controlling glare while keeping a view outside.
rows.light: Fabric openness affects visibility and light control. View-through fabrics may need another layer for nighttime privacy.
rows.planning: Compare samples at the window to judge the view and privacy you’ll have.

rows.reason: Adding insulation at a large area of glass.
rows.light: Light-filtering and room-darkening fabric choices suit different rooms.
rows.planning: Compare the shade’s pleated appearance and how much glass it covers when raised. Selected configurations also open sideways for doors.

rows.reason: A soft, drapery-like appearance across wide windows or sliding doors.
rows.light: Rotating fabric vanes let you adjust light and privacy while the sheer fabric softens daylight.
rows.planning: Allow space for the treatment to gather at the side when open.

rows.reason: Broad fabric panels with a contemporary look for wide or tall openings.
rows.light: Fabric opacity determines how much light comes through and how much privacy the panels provide.
rows.planning: Panels glide sideways and stack together. Their resting position should work with the view, furniture and door access.

sections.note: Available sizes, fabrics and controls vary by configuration. We’ll measure your opening and help you compare the combinations that fit your windows.

sections.heading: Look at the window treatment when it’s open
paragraphs: It’s easy to focus on how a treatment looks across the glass. Give some attention to where it goes when you open it.
A raised shade occupies space at the top of the window. Drapery and sliding panels gather at the sides. The amount of space they use affects how much glass remains visible.

With drapery, we look at the rod or track, the fabric fullness and where the panels will rest. Stationary side panels can frame the window, while a shade handles the everyday light control. Curtains that close across the opening need their own allowance for coverage and movement.
Window depth, handles, trim and nearby furniture also affect the fit. These details are part of measuring for the complete treatment.

sections.heading: Choose controls you’ll be comfortable using
paragraphs: Large windows often put controls out of easy reach, especially behind furniture or above a stairway.

Motorized operation lets you adjust compatible treatments without reaching each window. We work with Hunter Douglas PowerView and Somfy systems, and can explain the controls available with the shades you’re considering.

Power deserves attention too. With a rechargeable system, consider how you’ll reach the charging connection. For a hardwired installation, the power connection needs to be coordinated with the selected system. We’ll talk through those requirements as part of the product choice.

sections.heading: Compare samples beside your own windows
paragraphs: A fabric sample can look different against a bright window than it does on a table. Seeing it in your room helps you judge the color, texture and light coming through it.
During a free in-home consultation, we bring samples, take measurements and help you compare suitable options within your budget. You can also arrange an appointment at our Woodland Hills showroom.
Call (818) 884-5464 to talk about your windows or request a visit.
